rejected.title: Active and passive voice
card: Active voice
The doer comes first, then the action, then the receiver. Example: The dog chased the cat.
Passive voice
The receiver comes first. The verb is usually a form of be plus a past form of the verb. Example: The cat was chased by the dog.
In the passive, the doer can be left out. Example: The cat was chased. Now the reader does not know who did it.
A writer may choose the passive to put the focus on the receiver, or to hide who was responsible. The active makes the doer clear and the sentence direct.
rejected.remember: Active names the doer first. Passive puts the receiver first and can hide the doer.

a.q: In which sentence does the receiver of the action come first?
opts: The window was smashed during the storm
The storm smashed the window on Friday
Strong winds smashed the old window
The window smashed under the heavy hail
a.why: The window is the receiver and it comes first, with was smashed after it. In the other options the doer or the thing acting comes first. The last option can look passive, but the window is the one that smashed, not something done to it.
a.clue: Look for the thing the action is done to, placed at the start.

b.q: A school newsletter says: "Mistakes were made when the excursion money was counted." Why might the writer have chosen this wording?
opts: It leaves out who made the mistakes
It names the person who made the mistakes
It makes the sentence more direct and active
It shows the writer is very certain
b.why: Both verbs are passive, and neither names a doer, so the reader is not told who was responsible. An active sentence such as "The office staff made mistakes" would name the doer and be more direct. Certainty is a matter of modality, not voice.
b.clue: Does the sentence say who made the mistakes?

version.title: Active and passive voice
card: Active voice
the doer of the action comes first. In "The coach picked the team", the coach is the doer and the team receives the action.
Passive voice
the receiver comes first, and the verb is a form of be with a past participle, such as picked or eaten. In "The team was picked by the coach", the team comes first.
In the passive, the doer can be left out: "The team was picked." The reader is no longer told who made the choice.
Writers may use the passive to keep the focus on the receiver, or to hide who was responsible. The active voice makes the doer clear and the sentence direct.
version.remember: Active puts the doer first. Passive puts the receiver first and can leave the doer out.

a.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
opts: The fence was painted by Leo
Leo painted the old fence
Leo was painting the fence
Leo has painted the fence
a.why: The fence receives the action and comes first, with was plus the past participle painted. Leo was painting the fence uses was too, but Leo, the doer, still comes first, so it is active.
a.clue: Who or what comes first: the doer or the receiver?

b.q: A factory's report says: "The river was polluted last year." Why might the factory have chosen this wording?
opts: To avoid saying who polluted the river
To make clear that it caused the pollution
To put the doer first so it sounds direct
To show the pollution is still happening
b.why: The sentence is passive and names no doer, so readers are not told who caused the pollution. An active sentence such as "Our factory polluted the river" would put the doer first and make the blame clear.
b.clue: Does the sentence say who did the polluting?
